name: Bianca Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Bianca. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Halden Smart Homes, a small installer on the edge of town. We fit smart lighting, alarms, cameras and heating controls, plus all the normal stuff like new fuse boards when the old ones can't cope. I use an AI assistant every day, to write the setup guides for customers and to programme the lighting scenes, which used to take me an hour of fiddling. The best part is when an older customer realises they can turn the hall light on from bed. The worst is chasing Wi-Fi faults that aren't even ours.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And at home, how are things?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner, Sami, who's a trainee accountant at a firm in town. We just moved into a bigger rented flat, and his exam fees came out the same month, so savings are about three weeks' worth. My pay's lower than the bigger firms, but there aren't many of those nearby. We're okay, just stretched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. That surprises me a bit, given how much I already use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still useful, just not magic, which is what I've been saying for a while. At work I'd keep using it for the boring bits. Online I'd probably share a few tips on the installers' forum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a relief for Sami more than for me. His firm keeps talking about AI doing the bookkeeping, and if that stays small, his training's worth something. For me, the bigger worry is the rent, which went up when we moved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for setup guides and programming, and I'd offer to set up smart heating for a couple of neighbours on Saturdays for cash. I'd also look at the rent, because we stretched for this flat. Sami and I would set up a joint savings pot, even fifty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a bit stretched. The money stuff hums along in the background, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you charge the neighbours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About sixty for a heating controller install and an hour of setup. I'd keep it small, nothing that clashes with Halden's work. It's mostly older people who don't want to call a big company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why did you stretch for this flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sami's asthma was getting worse. The old flat had black mould in the bedroom, so stretching for the new one was worth it, but it left us with nothing behind us.

say: I'd say AI is **useful, not magic**, as I've been saying for a while.
I'd share **practical tips** on the installers' online forum.
think: A modest AI is a **relief for my partner**, a trainee accountant.
My bigger worry is the **rent rise** after we moved.
do: Keep using AI for **setup guides** and lighting programming.
Do **Saturday heating installs** for neighbours at about sixty each.
Start a **joint savings pot** with her partner, even fifty a month.
feel: Mostly **fine** but **stretched**, with money worries humming in the background.
S0.quote: The old flat had black mould in the bedroom, so stretching for the new one was worth it, but it left us with nothing behind us.
fieldNote: She's a **daily AI user** and calm about it staying modest.
Her thoughts go first to her **partner's exposure** as a trainee accountant.
The **flat move** for health reasons explains the thin cushion.
A small **side income** is her instinctive response, even in a calm world.

steps.text: Keep using AI to write setup guides and lighting scenes
Install smart heating for neighbours on Saturdays for cash
Open a joint savings pot with Sami for fifty monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking and planning. That's Sami's job, pretty much word for word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and people should learn the tools early. At work I'd be the one showing the older lads how to quote faster. Online I'd say the trades are a good bet, especially smart home work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job gets better and Sami's gets scary. Half of what trainee accountants do is checking and reconciling, which is exactly what the card says goes. So I could be doing fine at work and still have the household take a hit when my partner's accounting job shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help Sami think about switching to something more hands-on or advisory, maybe even an electrical apprenticeship. I'd push Halden to let me run the smart home programming side as a proper service. And I'd grow the Saturday work so we have a second income stream if Sami's hours drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not for me. It's a weird feeling, being the safe one in a couple.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Sami take the idea of an apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd laugh at first, then think about it. He's good with his hands, he built half our furniture. But he's spent two years on accountancy exams, and walking away from that would sting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if his income dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, probably, since I've got the work van. Then eating out. We'd be fine on my wage for a few months, but only just, with the new rent.

say: I'd tell people to **learn the tools early**.
I'd say online that **smart home work** is a good bet in the trades.
think: My job gets better while my partner's **checking and reconciling** work is exposed.
I could do fine while the **household** still takes a hit.

Grow the **Saturday work** into a second income.
feel: **Anxious** for her partner, and oddly the **safe one** in the couple.

fieldNote: Her anxiety is about the **household**, not her own job.

steps.text: Pitch smart home programming as a paid Halden service

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028. That's really soon. And robots by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say be practical, get skills that need hands, and don't wait for the government to catch up. At work I'd be calm and helpful, showing people what they can do. Online I'd probably say less, because everyone would be shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, Sami's job is gone in 2028, more or less. Mine lasts until about 2031, when robots that can fit a camera on a wall show up. So we'd have three years of me as the only reliable wage, and then we'd both be looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get Sami onto an electrical apprenticeship the first month, so he's qualified by the time I'm under pressure. I'd learn to programme and look after home robots, because someone will have to set them up in people's houses. And we'd move somewhere cheaper, even with the mould risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. And a bit guilty, because I've been telling everyone AI's fine, it just makes my job easier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move even with the mould risk. Would you really?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look harder, maybe at a place with my sister in the next town, who's got a spare room. We'd pay her something. It's not ideal, but it's better than a nice flat we can't afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would those three years feel like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Busy, I think, because everyone would want their homes set up for the new gadgets. I'd be working all hours and coming home to Sami doing coursework at the kitchen table. Honestly, it might be a good few years, before the hard ones.

say: I'd tell people to get **hands-on skills** and not wait for government.
I'd stay **calm and helpful** at work and quieter online.
think: My partner's job is **gone in 2028**, and mine lasts until about 2031.
That leaves **three years** of me as the only reliable wage.
do: Start her partner on an **electrical apprenticeship** in the first month.
Learn to **programme home robots**, since someone must set them up.
Move somewhere **cheaper**, possibly into her sister's spare room.
feel: A bit **guilty** for telling everyone AI only made her job easier.
S2.quote: We'd have three years of me as the only reliable wage, and then we'd both be looking.
fieldNote: She clearly maps the **robot lag**: her job outlives her partner's by three years.
Her plan is **active and quick**: retrain her partner, learn robot setup.
Moving in with her **sister** is a real fallback.
She admits **guilt** over her earlier relaxed public line on AI.

steps.text: Enrol Sami on an electrical apprenticeship within a month
Learn to programme and maintain home robots
Move into her sister's spare room in the next town

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Robots by 2034. That's a bit more doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to adjust if you start now, and I'd mean it. At work I'd push to be the person who handles the home robot installs when they start. Online I'd share how-to guides, the way I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for Sami to qualify as an electrician or switch to something safer. Two trades between us by 2034 is not safe, but it's a lot better than one accountant and one sparky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Sami and plan his switch over the first year, maybe finishing one more exam first. I'd start a proper side business with the smart home work, using AI for bookings and invoices. And I'd save, aiming for two months of rent by 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but organised. It feels like a project, not a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would Sami finish one more exam first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it gives him a qualification he can use for small firms' books, even if AI does most of it. It's a backstop. Then he moves to the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the side business look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A website, a booking assistant, me on Saturdays and some evenings. Smart heating, lighting, cameras, and later robot setup. Halden knows, and we'd agree I stay off their customers.

say: I'd say there's **time to adjust** if you start now.
I'd push to handle **home robot installs** at Halden when they start.
think: Five years lets my partner **qualify as an electrician** or switch safely.
**Two trades** between us is far better than one accountant and one electrician.
do: Plan her partner's **career switch** over the first year.
Start a **smart home side business** using AI for bookings and invoices.
feel: **Anxious** but organised, more like a project than a disaster.
S3.quote: Two trades between us by 2034 is not safe, but it's a lot better than one accountant and one sparky.
fieldNote: Five years lets her treat the change as a **household project**.
She keeps a **backstop** for her partner: one more accounting exam.
Her side business is **automated from the start** with AI tools.
Anxious rather than alarmed because **the plan feels doable**.

steps.text: Plan Sami's move into the electrical trade within a year
Launch a smart home side business with an AI booking assistant
Save two months of rent by 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay, that's much better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's a decade, so let's use it well. At work I'd keep pushing the smart home side and offer to train the others. I'd tell friends it's a good time to get into the trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one feels okay for us. Sami could finish his qualifications and still switch with time to spare. By 2039 I'd be thirty-nine, possibly with my own small firm, and with a decade to prepare, robots would be something I install, not something that replaces me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the side business slowly over three or four years, and only go full time when it's paying the rent. I'd learn robotics setup when the first proper courses appear. And Sami and I might start thinking about kids around thirty-two, which we'd put off in the faster versions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly positive. There's still the rent and the stretch, but this one has room for a life in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. How does the timeline change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two-year version, no way, we'd be scrambling. In this one we could plan it, maybe with my own business giving me flexible hours. It's funny how much the date matters for something so personal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could still go wrong in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Halden could get bought by a big chain and squeeze us, or the rent could jump again. Normal stuff. AI's the background in this one, not the main story.

say: I'd say there's **a decade**, so let's use it well.
I'd tell friends it's a **good time** to get into the trades.
think: With ten years, my partner can **finish qualifications** and still switch in time.
By 2039 I could run **my own firm**, installing robots rather than replaced by them.
do: Grow the **side business** slowly, going full time only when it pays rent.
Learn **robotics setup** when proper courses appear.
feel: **Uneasy** but mostly positive, with room for a life.
S4.quote: With a decade to prepare, robots would be something I install, not something that replaces me.
fieldNote: A decade makes **family plans** possible again for her.
She'd **grow the business** cautiously despite being comfortable with risk.
Her remaining worries are **ordinary**: rent and a possible takeover.
Uneasy, not calm, because **thin savings** still leave the couple exposed.

steps.text: Grow the smart home side business until it covers rent
Take a robotics setup course when one appears

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Sami's job goes almost straight away and mine follows three years later, and we've got no savings to cover the gap. What would help is funding for people to retrain into trades, so people like Sami can switch without losing a year's income, and some help with rent while they do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about couples where one job is safer than the other. Being the safe one is its own kind of pressure, because you end up carrying the plan for both of you.

headlineQuote: Being the safe one is its own kind of pressure, because you end up carrying the plan for both of you.
portrait: Bianca is a **27-year-old electrician** at a small smart home installer, fitting lighting, alarms and heating controls.
She uses **AI every day** to programme lighting scenes and write customer setup guides.
She lives with her partner, a **trainee accountant** whose work is highly exposed to AI.
With **three weeks** of savings after a health-driven move, she reaches quickly for side income.
Her worry centres on the **household**, and she plans to move her partner into the trades.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her partner's job goes first and hers follows three years later, with no savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Funded retraining** so people can switch into trades without losing a year's income.
**Rent support** while a household member retrains.
